name: The Alchemist
blurb: Paulo Coelho's fable of a Spanish shepherd who crosses the desert to follow a dream
title: The Alchemist Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending Explained
description: The Alchemist summary: Santiago, Melchizedek, Fatima and the alchemist, his journey from Spain to the pyramids, where the treasure really is and what it means.
h1: The Alchemist: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: The Alchemist (O Alquimista) is a 1988 novel by the Brazilian writer Paulo Coelho, first published in Portuguese; the English translation followed in 1993. It follows Santiago, a young shepherd from Andalusia in Spain, who has a recurring dream of treasure hidden at the Egyptian pyramids. Encouraged by a mysterious king, he sells his flock and travels through North Africa and across the Sahara. Told as a simple fable, the book is about pursuing what Coelho calls a Personal Legend, the thing a person most wants to do with their life.

body: Part One: Santiago sleeps with his sheep in an abandoned church where a sycamore grows through the ruined sacristy, and for the second time dreams that a child leads him to the pyramids and shows him hidden treasure. In the town of Tarifa an old fortune-teller tells him to go to Egypt and asks for one tenth of whatever he finds. In a town square an old man introduces himself as Melchizedek, king of Salem. He knows Santiago's past, explains the idea of a Personal Legend and the principle that when you want something, the universe helps you achieve it, and asks for a tenth of the flock. In return he gives Santiago two stones, Urim and Thummim, to read omens when he cannot decide. Santiago sells his sheep and sails to Tangier in Morocco.

Part Two: On his first day in Tangier a man who offered to guide him steals all his money. Santiago takes a job with a crystal merchant whose shop is failing. His ideas, such as displaying the glassware outside and selling tea in crystal glasses, make the merchant rich, while the merchant admits he never made his own pilgrimage to Mecca for fear of having nothing left to live for. After almost a year Santiago has enough money to buy twice as many sheep and go home, but he decides to continue to Egypt.

He joins a caravan crossing the Sahara, where he meets an Englishman reading books on alchemy who hopes to find a famous alchemist living at the oasis of Al-Fayoum. Tribal wars slow the caravan. At the oasis Santiago falls in love with Fatima, who tells him a woman of the desert waits for her man to return, and urges him to continue. Watching two hawks fight, he has a vision of an army attacking the oasis. He warns the chieftains, who prepare, and the attack is defeated; Santiago is rewarded with gold and offered a post as the oasis's counselor.

The alchemist, who has been watching him, appears and offers to guide him to the pyramids. He teaches Santiago to listen to his heart and to understand the Soul of the World. In the desert they are captured by a warring tribe, and the alchemist tells the chieftain that Santiago can turn himself into the wind. After three days of fear, Santiago speaks to the desert, the wind and the sun, and finally to the Hand that wrote all, and a huge windstorm rises; the tribe lets them go. At a Coptic monastery the alchemist turns lead into gold, gives Santiago a share, leaves another share with the monk in case Santiago needs it, and departs.

At the pyramids Santiago weeps, sees a scarab beetle where his tears fall, and starts digging. Men fleeing the tribal wars find him, beat him and take his gold. When he explains that a dream sent him there, their leader laughs and says he too once dreamed of treasure, buried under a sycamore in a ruined church in Spain where shepherds sleep, but he was not foolish enough to cross the desert for a dream.

Santiago now knows where the treasure is. In the epilogue he returns to the church in Spain, digs beneath the sycamore and finds a chest of old Spanish gold coins and precious stones. He plans to take one tenth to the fortune-teller, as promised. The wind brings him the scent of Fatima's perfume, and he tells her he is coming back to her.

The treasure was at home all along, but Santiago could not have found it without the journey: only the thief's dream, heard at the pyramids, tells him where to dig. Readers usually take this in two compatible ways. One is that the journey itself is the real treasure, because Santiago gains love, knowledge and confidence along the way. The other, stressed in the book through the crystal merchant and the thief, is that ignoring your dream is the only true failure; both men had the same signs as Santiago but chose not to act. Critics have also read the book less kindly, as a simple self-help message wrapped in a fable, and that debate is part of its reputation.

ul: The Personal Legend: each person has a destiny, and Santiago's journey shows the cost and reward of following it.
Omens and the Soul of the World: signs such as the hawks and the scarab guide Santiago once he learns to read them.
Fear: the crystal merchant and the thief show how fear of failure stops people from pursuing their dreams.
Love: Fatima supports Santiago's quest instead of holding him back, and love is presented as part of the journey.
Alchemy as self-transformation: turning lead into gold stands for a person becoming the best version of themselves.
Length: a short novel of under 200 pages in most English editions, divided into two parts, a prologue and an epilogue.
Original language: Portuguese; the English translation appeared in 1993, and the book has been translated into more than 65 languages.
Sources: the core plot, a man who travels far to find a treasure that was buried at home, is an old folktale, and a version of it appears in the One Thousand and One Nights.
What teachers usually ask about: the meaning of Personal Legend, the role of omens, and why the treasure turns out to be back in Spain.

options: Under a sycamore in the ruined church in Spain
check.why: The thief's dream reveals that the treasure lies in the church where Santiago first had his dream.

faq.q: What is a Personal Legend in The Alchemist?
faq.a: It is the book's term for a person's true calling, the thing they have always wanted to accomplish; Melchizedek says everyone knows theirs when young but most people give it up.
The book ends before that happens. After finding the treasure, Santiago smells her perfume on the wind and says he is coming back to her.

faq.q: Is The Alchemist based on a true story?
faq.a: No. It is a fable built on an old folktale about a man who travels to find treasure that was at home all along; a version appears in the One Thousand and One Nights.
